title: UML Sequence and Other Diagrams
summary: Showing behavior over time with lifelines and messages, and knowing when a second diagram type is actually worth the interview time it costs to draw.

slides.markdown:
A class diagram freezes a design's *structure* — what the classes are and how they're related. A **sequence diagram** shows *behavior over time* — the exact order messages fly between objects to carry out one use case, like "place an order."

They're drawn far less often than class diagrams because they cost more time for less payoff, so the real skill here is judgment: knowing the notation well enough to draw it fast, and knowing when it's actually worth drawing at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Sequence diagrams: lifelines, activation bars, messages, in interview shorthand
slides.markdown:
A sequence diagram has one **lifeline** per object — a labeled box at the top with a dashed vertical line running down, representing that object existing over time. A thin rectangle on a lifeline, called an **activation bar**, marks the span during which that object is actively doing work (running a method). Horizontal arrows between lifelines are **messages** — method calls — and time flows top to bottom, so the arrow closest to the top happens first.

Interview shorthand drops formal activation bars entirely on a fast whiteboard: just lifelines and arrows, in order, is usually enough to convey the flow. Add activation bars only when nesting genuinely needs the extra clarity — for example, an object calling out to a second object while still mid-call to a first.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a sequence diagram for "place an order" across three objects
slides.markdown:
```
Client -> OrderService : createOrder()
OrderService -> PaymentService : charge(amount)
PaymentService --> OrderService : paymentOk
OrderService --> Client : orderConfirmed
```

Read it top to bottom: the `Client` calls `createOrder()` on `OrderService`, which calls out to `PaymentService.charge()`, waits for `paymentOk` to come back (the dashed `-->` return arrows), and only then replies `orderConfirmed` to the original caller. The nesting is the point — `OrderService` can't confirm the order until its own call to `PaymentService` returns.

slides.sectionTitle: Sync vs async messages, and return messages
slides.markdown:
A **synchronous** message (solid line, filled arrowhead `───▶`) means the caller blocks until the callee finishes and replies — the typical method call. An **asynchronous** message (solid line, open arrowhead `───▷`) means the caller fires off the message and keeps going without waiting — a queued job, a fire-and-forget event. A **return message** (dashed line, open arrowhead `┈┈▷`) shows a value coming back from a call that already happened.

Mixing these up changes what the diagram claims about your system: drawing `OrderService → NotificationService` as synchronous implies order confirmation waits on an email actually sending, which is usually not the design you intend. If a step should happen in the background, draw it async — the arrow style is doing real communicative work, not just decoration.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a brief activity diagram for a decision-heavy flow
slides.markdown:
Unlike a sequence diagram, an **activity diagram** shows a flow of logic and decisions rather than which object talks to which. Rounded boxes are actions, diamonds are decisions, and a filled circle marks the start.

```
(start)
   |
   v
[Validate order]
   |
   v
<In stock?> --No--> [Notify: out of stock] --> (end)
   | Yes
   v
[Charge payment]
   |
   v
<Payment ok?> --No--> [Notify: payment failed] --> (end)
   | Yes
   v
[Confirm order] --> (end)
```

This is the shape to reach for when the interesting part of a use case is *branching logic*, not which service calls which — a sequence diagram would bury these decisions inside prose notes instead of showing them structurally.

slides.sectionTitle: When a sequence diagram is worth drawing vs when it's overkill
slides.markdown:
Draw a sequence diagram when the interview question is specifically about *interaction order* — who calls whom, what waits on what, where a race condition or double-call could sneak in. "Walk me through what happens when a payment times out" is a sequence-diagram question: the ordering and the retry are the whole point.

Skip it when a class diagram plus one sentence already answers the question. "How does OrderService relate to PaymentService" doesn't need lifelines — a single association arrow says it. Drawing a sequence diagram anyway signals you're padding for time rather than picking the tool the question actually calls for.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: class diagram (structure) vs sequence diagram (behavior over time) — which to draw first
slides.markdown:
| | Class diagram | Sequence diagram |
|---|---|---|
| Shows | Structure — classes, relationships, multiplicities | Behavior — the order messages fly for one use case |
| Time axis | None — a static snapshot | Explicit — top to bottom is chronological |
| Best for | "What are the pieces and how do they relate?" | "What actually happens, step by step, when X occurs?" |
| Interview cost | Cheap — a few minutes | Expensive — easy to over-detail and run long |

**How to decide:** draw the class diagram first, always — you can't sequence messages between objects that don't exist yet on paper. Reach for a sequence diagram second, and only if the question is specifically about ordering, timing, or a failure mode in that ordering.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a sequence diagram so detailed it eats the whole interview clock
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A more detailed sequence diagram — every getter, every internal helper call — proves I understand the system deeply."

**Why it's wrong:** an interview has a fixed clock, and every extra lifeline or message is time not spent discussing trade-offs, failure modes, or scaling — the parts that actually differentiate a strong answer. A diagram so granular it takes five minutes to draw has usually crossed from "communicating clearly" into "stalling."

**Correct model:** include only the objects and calls that matter to the question being asked — typically 3-5 lifelines and the messages that cross a real system boundary (network call, queue, external service). Internal method calls within one object almost never belong on the diagram.
